channel.title: Acme: Light News
channel.description: Positive, lighthearted and unusual current news.

item.title: Medieval chain mail surfaces from a 1495 royal shipwreck
item.description: Divers exploring Denmark’s royal flagship Gribshunden, which sank in 1495 off Sweden, recovered fragments of copper-alloy chain mail. Researchers think the armor may have belonged to German mercenaries traveling with King Hans, adding a tactile clue to life aboard a Renaissance warship.

item.title: Teachers discover Texas’ second known buffalo jump
item.description: A group of science teachers hiking in Caprock Canyons found hundreds of bison bones below a cliff, leading archaeologists to identify only the second buffalo jump documented in Texas. Evidence suggests Indigenous hunters used the site for roughly 3,000 years.

item.title: New book introduces 60 of New York’s bodega cats
item.description: Bodega Cats of New York collects portraits and stories of 60 shop cats from all five boroughs. Dan Rimada’s profiles and Gulce Kilkis’ 150 photographs turn the familiar counter-top guardians into neighborhood characters, with 240 pages devoted to cats, stores and the people who care for them.

item.title: Kiwi return to Wellington’s hills after more than 150 years
item.description: More than 250 kiwi now roam the hills around New Zealand’s capital after a Māori-led project deployed 5,300 traps across nearly 60,000 acres to control stoats. Capital Kiwi says chick survival has topped 90% under the program, restoring the flightless birds to a landscape where they had been absent for more than 150 years.

item.title: ‘Retired’ parakeet pair surprise keepers with a new family
item.description: Sophia and Prince Polo, two orange-fronted parakeets thought to be past breeding age, produced chicks at Christchurch’s Orana Wildlife Park—and Sophia laid another clutch a month later. The critically endangered New Zealand species has twice been declared extinct and numbers only about 450 birds.

item.title: Volunteers turn difficult cursive letters into searchable history
item.description: Volunteers at Bowling Green State University are deciphering handwritten letters and converting them into searchable text. The project makes fragile records easier for researchers and the public to discover while giving people who still read cursive a practical way to preserve women’s history and other stories locked in archives.

item.title: Bagot goats take on a steep conservation job in Greenwich Park
item.description: Britain’s oldest native goat breed is spending November 23–27 browsing thorny growth below the Royal Observatory. The small, sure-footed Bagot goats can reach Castle Hill Bank where machines and volunteers struggle, helping protect a famous view while making room for more plant life.

item.title: Conservation partners return the 1,000th Jamaican rock iguana to the wild
item.description: A November 14 release of 33 iguanas in Jamaica’s Hellshire Hills pushed a decades-long recovery program past 1,000 animals returned to the wild. The species was thought extinct until 1990. Head-starting now gives hatchlings time to grow before they face predators in their native dry forest.

item.title: Four rescued manatees head back to Florida for the final leg of rehabilitation
item.description: Redrock, Rosalyn, Erie and Hundo traveled safely from Ohio zoos to Florida rehabilitation centers, bringing each closer to a winter release in native waters. Custom foam-lined crates, blankets, misting and careful air-and-road coordination kept the large passengers comfortable along the way.

item.title: New Zealand’s longest lizards return home after 30 years
item.description: Eleven threatened niho taniwha, or chevron skinks, have returned to Aotea/Great Barrier Island after three decades at Auckland Zoo. The 30-centimeter lizards were released into predator-controlled forest with bamboo refuges and tiny radio transmitters, joining ten others returned in July.

item.title: Zeus the cat commutes 37 miles to London and back
item.description: Four-year-old Zeus boarded an evening train in Braintree and rode 37 miles to London Liverpool Street. Station staff kept the seasoned traveler safe in their office, then a Greater Anglia employee escorted him home. His owner says the sociable cat wears two trackers and has caught trains before.

item.title: Otters bring hope to Kuala Lumpur’s once-filthy river
item.description: Families of vulnerable smooth-coated otters are turning up along Kuala Lumpur’s Klang River, once rated in Malaysia’s worst pollution class. Years of cleanup have improved the river to moderately polluted, and conservationists hope the playful fish-eaters will rally support for cleaner water and restored banks.

item.title: Shuri Castle’s main hall rises again in Okinawa
item.description: Seven years after a fire destroyed Shuri Castle’s main buildings, Okinawa unveiled the rebuilt Seiden main hall. Its deep-red exterior and dragon ornaments again crown the former Ryukyu Kingdom site, a treasured symbol of the islands’ distinct history. The public opening begins Monday while restoration continues.

item.title: Orphaned baby marmoset finds a surrogate mum named Minty
item.description: A five-month-old marmoset rescued from a London garden shed has been named Gino after the police officer who found him. Weighing just 140 grams and showing early rickets, he is recovering at Monkey World in Dorset, where an adult marmoset named Minty has taken him under her wing.

item.title: Whale breath gives scientists whole genomes without a biopsy
item.description: Researchers used drones to collect misty “blow” from humpback whales and sequence entire genomes without touching the animals. Among 58 samples from 26 whales, the breath DNA closely matched traditional biopsies and revealed three previously undocumented mitochondrial variants, offering a gentler tool for conservation.
